entities.summary:
The Battle of Culloden, fought on April 27, 1746, was the final confrontation of the Jacobite rising of 1745 and part of a religious civil war in Britain. Charles Edward Stuart, also known as Bonnie Prince Charlie, led the Jacobite forces against the British government, while the Duke of Cumberland commanded the government forces. The battle took place in Culloden, Scotland, and marked the end of the Jacobite dream of restoring the Stuart monarchy to power in Britain.

The Jacobite army, which included Highland regiments and French and Spanish mercenaries, was defeated by the British army, which consisted of English, Scottish, and Irish troops. The British forces were better trained and equipped, and they used their advantage in artillery to devastating effect. The Jacobite army was also hampered by poor leadership and divisions within the ranks.

The Battle of Culloden was a significant event in British history, marking the end of the Jacobite rising and the beginning of a long period of British dominance over Scotland. It also marked the end of the traditional way of life in the Highlands, as the British government imposed its authority and suppressed the Jacobite movement. The battle had a lasting impact on Scotland, leading to the forced eviction of many Highlanders from their lands and the suppression of their culture.

The Jacobite dream of restoring the Stuart monarchy to power in Britain was crushed, but the memory of the battle lived on, inspiring artists, writers, and musicians for generations to come. The battle has become a symbol of Scottish pride and resistance, a reminder of the long struggle for Scottish independence and self-determination.
